title: Setting a Work Schedule to Make Us Better, Saner Teachers
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that teachers should constrain their working hours, drawing on the story of Dr. Seuss writing Green Eggs and Ham under a 50-word limit to show that constraints can produce breakthroughs. He extends the point to curricular constraints, suggesting teachers save stress by pursuing students' flourishing within them instead of constantly fighting them. Since motivation alone does not get work done, he leans on Duhigg's habit research and lays out his own daily schedule in detail: protected morning prep without email, a cap of two meetings per week during prep, an 'intentionally interruptible' hour after school, and a final block in which he treats himself as gone and works behind a closed door. He refuses to bring work home, apart from a short Sunday-night prep block, so he can be present with his family. He closes by urging readers to design their own schedules for greater efficiency, effectiveness and sanity.
points: Stuart uses the Green Eggs and Ham story to argue that constraints, including self-imposed limits on work hours, can produce breakthroughs.
He contends that habit, not motivation, gets work done, so a fixed weekly schedule matters more than good intentions.
His prep-period rule caps meetings at two per week, on the grounds that professionals are not incessantly available because they have work to do.
Staying late only helps if you 'treat yourself as if you're gone': closing the door and working on the most important tasks rather than socializing.
His no-work-at-home rule protects time with family, apart from a single Sunday-evening prep block.
quotes: The point? Constraints can create breakthroughs we wouldn't otherwise have had without the constraints in place.

But we teachers can save ourselves a lot of stress by determining to promote the long-term flourishing of our students within some of the curricular or assessment constraints placed upon us, rather than constantly seeking to buck them.
As I'm learning in Charles Duhigg's The Power of Habit, getting things done requires way more than motivation or drive — it requires habit. And that's where my routine comes in.

Ideally, this time is dedicated to what its name implies: preparing for future instruction. Meetings can sometimes contribute to this, but meetings alone can't get it done. That's reflected in the limits I place on my meeting availability below. Remember: we are professionals. Professionals aren't incessantly available because, you know, they have work to do.

It's 3:30pm. At this point, a lot of teachers go home. I don't because I've been in the place where teacher work bleeds into everything, and so I no longer bring work home. When I go home, I want to relate, to connect, to just be.

However, simply staying at work doesn't mean you get anything done. Many teachers stay at school until 5:20 like me, but they get next to jack done on a regular basis. The key, I've found, is treating yourself as if you're gone.
I sincerely urge you to invest some time before break ends to start thinking about a schedule you can use to force you into greater efficiency, effectiveness, and sanity as a teacher and a human.
